verses.zh: 雅各见埃及有粮，就对儿子们说：「你们为甚么彼此观望呢？
verses.en: When Jacob heard[NOTE:1] there was grain in Egypt, he[NOTE:2] said to his sons, “Why are you looking at each other?”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “saw.”
Heb “Jacob.” Here the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

Why are you looking at each other? The point of Jacob’s question is that his sons should be going to get grain rather than sitting around doing nothing. Jacob, as the patriarch, still makes the decisions for the whole clan.
verses.commentary:
42:1 "Now Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt" The VERB "see" is used twice in
Gen. 42:1.

- "Jacob saw," BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERFECT with waw

- "Why are you staring at one another," Hithpael IMPERFECT

This same word is used of Pharaoh's dream (cf. Gen. 41:19,22,28) and by Joseph for Pharaoh to
look for a discerning and wise man (cf. Gen. 41:33). This common VERB is used in this chapter
several times (i.e., Gen. 42:1 [twice],7,9,12,21,27,35). Rashi says that he had a divine vision, but he
probably saw that others in Canaan were purchasing grain from Pharaoh (cf. Gen. 47:14).

verses.zh: 我听见埃及有粮，你们可以下去，从那里为我们籴些来，使我们可以存活，不至于死。」
verses.en: He then said, “Look, I hear that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy grain for us[NOTE:1] so that we may live[NOTE:2] and not die.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and buy for us from there.” The word “grain,” the direct object of “buy,” has been supplied for clarity, and the words “from there” have been omitted in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Following the imperatives, the prefixed verbal form with prefixed vav expresses purpose of result.
The imperfect tense continues the nuance of the verb before it.
verses.commentary:
42:2 Jacob commands his sons to go to Egypt to sustain (i.e., "live and not die") the family.

- go down there, BDB 432, KB 434, Qal IMPERATIVE

- buy some for us, BDB 991, KB 1404, Qal IMPERATIVE

- so that we may live, BDB 310, KB 309, Qal imperfect used
in a COHORTATIVE sense. The famine was pervasive and severe!

verses.zh: 于是，约瑟的十个哥哥都下埃及籴粮去了。
verses.en: So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
verses.commentary:
42:3-4 Jacob still did not trust the brothers. They had somehow been a part of Joseph's death and
he would not trust something similar to happen to Rachel's only remaining child, Benjamin.

verses.zh: 但约瑟的兄弟便雅悯，雅各没有打发他和哥哥们同去，因为雅各说：「恐怕他遭害。」
verses.en: But Jacob did not send Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers,[NOTE:1] for he said,[NOTE:2] “What if some accident[NOTE:3] happens[NOTE:4] to him?”
notes: Heb “But Benjamin, the brother of Joseph, Jacob did not send with his brothers.” The disjunctive clause highlights the contrast between Benjamin and the other ten.
The Hebrew verb אָמַר (ʾamar, “to say”) could also be translated “thought” (i.e., “he said to himself”) here, giving Jacob’s reasoning rather than spoken words.

The Hebrew noun אָסוֹן (ʾason) is a rare word meaning “accident, harm.” Apart from its use in these passages it occurs in Exodus 21:22-23 of an accident to a pregnant woman. The term is a rather general one, but Jacob was no doubt thinking of his loss of Joseph.
Heb “encounters.”
verses.commentary:
42:4 "that harm may befall him" The term "harm" (BDB 62) is rare (cf. Gen. 44:29; Exod. 21:22,23)
and implies a life-threatening accident. Jacob is fearful for the life of the only child of his beloved,
deceased Rachel (i.e., Benjamin, Joseph's younger full brother). One wonders if Jacob thought he would be
the leader of the family.

This VERB (BDB 896, II KB 1131, Qal IMPERFECT) is used
in a negative sense here and in Lev. 10:19; Deut. 31:29; Job 4:14; Isa. 51:19; Jer. 13:22; 44:23, and is
usually translated "befall."

verses.zh: 来籴粮的人中有以色列的儿子们，因为迦南地也有饥荒。
verses.en: So Israel’s sons came to buy grain among the other travelers,[NOTE:1] for the famine was severe in the land of Canaan.
notes: Heb “in the midst of the coming ones.”
verses.commentary:
42:5 "So the sons of Israel came to buy grain among those who were coming" Some wonder why
Jacob sent all of his sons (earlier he had divided his family for safety, cf. Gen. 32:22-32). It was possibly
because

- each individual could only buy so much grain

- that there was safety in numbers

▣ "for the famine was in the 1and of Canaan also" From history we know that famine
periodically swept through this part of the world (see IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 72. It was
caused by

- lack of rain at the appropriate time

- too much rain or cold

- insects

- blight, mildew

Canaan was dependant on regular natural cycles, but Egypt was dependant on the Nile
(i.e., flooding annually).

verses.zh: 当时治理埃及地的是约瑟；粜粮给那地众民的就是他。约瑟的哥哥们来了，脸伏于地，向他下拜。
verses.en: Now Joseph was the ruler of the country, the one who sold grain to all the people of the country.[NOTE:1] Joseph’s brothers came and bowed down[NOTE:2] before him with[NOTE:3] their faces to the ground.
notes: The disjunctive clause either introduces a new episode in the unfolding drama or provides the reader with supplemental information necessary to understanding the story.

Joseph’s brothers came and bowed down before him. Here is the beginning of the fulfillment of Joseph’s dreams (see Gen 37). But it is not the complete fulfillment, since all his brothers and his parents must come. The point of the dream, of course, was not simply to get the family to bow to Joseph, but that Joseph would be placed in a position of rule and authority to save the family and the world (41:57).
The word “faces” is an adverbial accusative, so the preposition has been supplied in the translation.
verses.commentary:
42:6 "And Joseph's brothers came and bowed down to him with their faces to the ground" Not only
does this verse seem to fulfill Joseph's dream of Gen. 37:6-9, but also 43:28; and 44:14.

verses.zh: 约瑟看见他哥哥们，就认得他们，却装作生人，向他们说些严厉话，问他们说：「你们从哪里来？」他们说：「我们从迦南地来籴粮。」
verses.en: When Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he pretended to be a stranger[NOTE:1] to them and spoke to them harshly. He asked, “Where do you come from?” They answered,[NOTE:2] “From the land of Canaan, to buy grain for food.”[NOTE:3]
notes: But pretended to be a stranger. Joseph intends to test his brothers to see if they have changed and have the integrity to be patriarchs of the tribes of Israel. He will do this by putting them in the same situations that they and he were in before. The first test will be to awaken their conscience.
Heb “said.”
The verb is denominative, meaning “to buy grain”; the word “food” could simply be the direct object, but may also be an adverbial accusative.
verses.commentary:
42:7 "he recognized them" The VERB "regard, "recognize" (BDB 647, KB 699) is used twice
in Gen. 42:7 (Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw, Hithpael
IMPERFECT) with waw and twice in Gen. 42:8 (Hiphil IMPERFECT
with waw, Hiphil PERFECT). They were still
bearded and dressed in the traditional garb of the nomadic tribes. On the other hand Joseph was clean shaven,
finely dressed, in a place of authority, and he spoke Egyptian. All of these things disguised him well
from his brothers.

▣ "he recognized. . .he disguised" Both of these VERBS come from the same root,
נכר.

- recognized, BDB 647, KB 699, Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw,
cf. Gen. 27:23; 37:33; 38:25,26; 42:7,8 (twice); Deut. 33:9

- disguised (lit. "treat as a stranger"), BDB 649, KB 699, Hithpael IMPERFECT
with waw, cf. 1 Kgs. 14:5,6

It is uncertain if there are two separate Hebrew roots or two usages.

▣

NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta
"harshly"

NKJV
"roughly"

LXX
"hard words"

NAB
"sternly"

The ADJECTIVE (BDB 904) means "hard," or "severe." It is used in
1 Sam. 25:3 to describe Nabal's personality. Here it describes the tone of Joseph's voice (cf. 1 Sam. 20:10),
as well as the content of his accusations (i.e., they were spies).

verses.zh: 约瑟认得他哥哥们，他们却不认得他。
verses.en: Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.

verses.zh: 约瑟想起从前所做的那两个梦，就对他们说：「你们是奸细，来窥探这地的虚实。」
verses.en: Then Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed about them, and he said to them, “You are spies;[NOTE:1] you have come to see if our land is vulnerable!”[NOTE:2]
notes: You are spies. Joseph wanted to see how his brothers would react if they were accused of spying.
Heb “to see the nakedness of the land you have come.”
verses.commentary:
42:9 "Joseph remembered the dreams" This refers to chapter 37. Joseph had named his first son
Manasseh ("making to forget"), but the memories of his brothers' betrayal came flooding back.

▣ "You are spies" The Rabbinical Midrash says that Jacob told his sons to enter the city by
different gates and that Joseph observed this and used it to accuse them of being spies (BDB 920, KB 1183,
Piel PARTICIPLE, cf. Jos. 2:1; 6:22-23; 1 Sam. 26:4). Joseph did this in order to
test their motives and character.

▣

NASB
"the undefended parts of the land"

NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA
"the nakedness of the land"

TEV
"where the country is weak"

NJB
"the country's weak points"

LXX
"the marks (i.e., scrutinize the tracks) of the land"

REB
"the weak points of our defences"

Peshitta
"a report about the land"

This term (BDB 788) is literally "naked" (cf. Gen. 9:22-23) or "bare." The sense here
(determined by the context) is the area of Egypt without forts or military guards. It is a false accusation
to test Jacob's children.

verses.zh: 他们对他说：「我主啊，不是的。仆人们是籴粮来的。
verses.en: But they exclaimed,[NOTE:1] “No, my lord! Your servants have come to buy grain for food!
notes: Heb “and they said to him.” In context this is best understood as an exclamation.

verses.zh: 我们都是一个人的儿子，是诚实人；仆人们并不是奸细。」
verses.en: We are all the sons of one man; we are honest men! Your servants are not spies.”
verses.commentary:
42:11 "we are honest men" "Honest" (BDB 467 II, cf. Gen. 42:11,19,31,34) is used in the sense of
irony of what they had earlier done to Joseph. They appeared as upright, forthright men, but they had
acted in evil ways (cf. Genesis 34,37).

verses.zh: 约瑟说：「不然，你们必是窥探这地的虚实来的。」
verses.en: “No,” he insisted, “but you have come to see if our land is vulnerable.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and he said, ‘No, for the nakedness of the land you have come to see.’” The order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 他们说：「仆人们本是弟兄十二人，是迦南地一个人的儿子，顶小的现今在我们的父亲那里，有一个没有了。」
verses.en: They replied, “Your servants are from a family of twelve brothers.[NOTE:1] We are the sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is with our father at this time,[NOTE:2] and one is no longer alive.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “twelve [were] your servants, brothers [are] we.”
Heb “today.”
Heb “and the one is not.”
verses.commentary:
42:13 "the sons of one man in the land of Canaan, and behold, the youngest is with our father today,
and one is no longer alive" The last phrase is obviously referring to Joseph. It is ironical that
they are speaking this to his face without knowing who he was.

verses.zh: 约瑟说：「我才说你们是奸细，这话实在不错。
verses.en: But Joseph told them, “It is just as I said to you:[NOTE:1] You are spies!
notes: Heb “to you, saying.”

verses.zh: 我指着法老的性命起誓，若是你们的小兄弟不到这里来，你们就不得出这地方，从此就可以把你们证验出来了。
verses.en: You will be tested in this way: As surely as Pharaoh lives,[NOTE:1] you will not depart from this place unless your youngest brother comes here.
notes: Heb “[By] the life of Pharaoh.”sn As surely as Pharaoh lives. Joseph uses an oath formula to let the brothers know the certainty of what he said. There is some discussion in the commentaries on swearing by the life of Pharaoh, but since the formulation here reflects the Hebrew practice, it would be hard to connect the ideas exactly to Egyptian practices. Joseph did this to make the point in a way that his Hebrew brothers would understand. See M. R. Lehmann, “Biblical Oaths,” ZAW 81 (1969): 74-92.
verses.commentary:
42:15 "by the life of Pharaoh" Many commentators have criticized Joseph for taking this oath twice.
It fits his disguise! He is obviously not using it in a theological sense. However, it is a reference to
the Egyptian tradition that Pharaoh was the son of the sun god, Re. This very oath has been found on Egyptian
monuments.

verses.zh: 须要打发你们中间一个人去，把你们的兄弟带来。至于你们，都要囚在这里，好证验你们的话真不真，若不真，我指着法老的性命起誓，你们一定是奸细。」
verses.en: One of you must go and get[NOTE:1] your brother, while[NOTE:2] the rest of you remain in prison.[NOTE:3] In this way your words may be tested to see if[NOTE:4] you are telling the truth.[NOTE:5] If not, then, as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!”
notes: Heb “send from you one and let him take.” After the imperative, the prefixed verbal form with prefixed vav (ו) indicates purpose.
The disjunctive clause is here circumstantial-temporal.
Heb “bound.”
The words “to see” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “the truth [is] with you.”
verses.commentary:
42:16 Joseph makes several commands and demands.

- send one of you, BDB 1018, KB 1511, Qal,IMPERATIVE

- that he may get your brother, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERFECT used in
a JUSSIVE sense

- while you remain in prison, BDB 63, KB 75, Niphal IMPERATIVE

- that your words be tested, BDB 103, KB 119, Niphal IMPERFECT used in
a JUSSIVE sense

verses.zh: 于是约瑟把他们都下在监里三天。
verses.en: He imprisoned[NOTE:1] them all for three days.
notes: The same Hebrew word is used for Joseph’s imprisonment in 40:3, 4, 7. There is some mirroring going on in the narrative. The Hebrew word used here (אָסַף, ʾasaf, “to gather”) is not normally used in a context like this (for placing someone in prison), but it forms a wordplay on the name Joseph (יוֹסֵף, yosef) and keeps the comparison working.
verses.commentary:
42:17 "So he put them all in the prison for three days" Apparently Joseph wanted them to experience
some of the agony that he had gone through at their expense.

verses.zh: 到第三天，约瑟对他们说：「我是敬畏　神的；你们照我的话行就可以存活。
verses.en: On the third day Joseph said to them, “Do as I say[NOTE:1] and you will live,[NOTE:2] for I fear God.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Do this.”
After the preceding imperative, the imperative with vav (ו) can, as here, indicate logical sequence.

For I fear God. Joseph brings God into the picture to awaken his brothers’ consciences. The godly person cares about the welfare of people, whether they live or die. So he will send grain back, but keep one of them in Egypt. This action contrasts with their crime of selling their brother into slavery.
verses.commentary:
42:18-20 Joseph's commands and demands continue.

- do this, Gen. 42:18, BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE

- live, Gen. 42:18, BDB 310, KB 309, Qal IMPERATIVE

- let one of your brothers be confined, Gen. 42:19, BDB 63, KB 75, Niphal
IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

- go, Gen. 42:19, BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE

- carry grain, Gen. 42:19, BDB 97, KB 112, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- bring your brother to me, Gen. 42:20, BDB 97, KB 112, Hiphil IMPERFECT
used in a JUSSIVE sense

- so your words may be verified, Gen. 42:20, BDB 52, KB 63, Niphal IMPERFECT
used in a JUSSIVE sense

42:18 "for I fear God" This phrase could relate to Joseph's oaths in Pharaoh's name (cf. Gen. 42:15,16)
or to his fear of the divine in general related to his charges against these ten men. Joseph is asserting,
in a roundabout way, his integrity and spirituality (cf. Gen. 20:11). He did fear/revere Elohim.

▣ "I fear God" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

verses.zh: 你们如果是诚实人，可以留你们中间的一个人囚在监里，但你们可以带着粮食回去，救你们家里的饥荒。
verses.en: If you are honest men, leave one of your brothers confined here in prison[NOTE:1] while the rest of you go[NOTE:2] and take grain back for your hungry families.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “bound in the house of your prison.”
The disjunctive clause is circumstantial-temporal.
Heb “[for] the hunger of your households.”

verses.zh: 把你们的小兄弟带到我这里来，如此，你们的话便有证据，你们也不至于死。」他们就照样而行。
verses.en: But you must bring[NOTE:1] your youngest brother to me. Then[NOTE:2] your words will be verified[NOTE:3] and you will not die.” They did as he said.[NOTE:4]
notes: The imperfect here has an injunctive force.
After the injunctive imperfect, this imperfect with vav indicates purpose or result.
The Niphal form of the verb has the sense of “to be faithful; to be sure; to be reliable.” Joseph will test his brothers to see if their words are true.
Heb “and they did so.”
verses.commentary:
42:20 "verified" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE,
TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

verses.zh: 他们彼此说：「我们在兄弟身上实在有罪。他哀求我们的时候，我们见他心里的愁苦，却不肯听，所以这场苦难临到我们身上。」
verses.en: They said to one another,[NOTE:1] “Surely we’re being punished[NOTE:2] because of our brother, because we saw how distressed he was[NOTE:3] when he cried to us for mercy, but we refused to listen. That is why this distress[NOTE:4] has come on us!”
notes: Heb “a man to his neighbor.”
Or “we are guilty”; the Hebrew word can also refer to the effect of being guilty, i.e., “we are being punished for guilt.”
Heb “the distress of his soul.”

The repetition of the Hebrew noun translated distress draws attention to the fact that they regard their present distress as appropriate punishment for their refusal to ignore their brother when he was in distress.
verses.commentary:
42:21 "They said to each other, 'we are truly guilty concerning our brother'" They felt that God
was punishing them because of their sin against Joseph. This is obvious from Gen. 42:21,22,28 and 44:16.
There is a sense that we reap what we sow (cf. Job 34:11; Ps. 28:4; 62:12; Pro. 24:12; Eccl. 12:14;
Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:6; 14:12; 1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:6-7; 2 Tim. 4:14;
1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12). However, there is also another biblical truth that God does not deal
with us according to our sins (cf. Ps. 103:10). We do not receive temporal punishment for all of our sins,
or we would all be dead and yet there are occasions when God does do this.

verses.zh: 流便说：「我岂不是对你们说过，不可伤害那孩子吗？只是你们不肯听，所以流他血的罪向我们追讨。」
verses.en: Reuben said to them, “Didn’t I say to you, ‘Don’t sin against the boy,’ but you wouldn’t listen? So now we must pay for shedding his blood!”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and also his blood, look, it is required.” God requires compensation, as it were, from those who shed innocent blood (see Gen 9:6). In other words, God exacts punishment for the crime of murder.
verses.commentary:
42:22 "Reuben answered them saying, 'Did I not tell you, "Do not sin against the boy"; and you would
not listen'" This is probably the first time that Joseph had ever heard that Reuben had tried to
defend him (cf. Gen. 37:22-24). Now these brothers believed that Joseph's innocent blood was crying out
for vengeance as Abel's blood did against his brother in Genesis 4.

verses.zh: 他们不知道约瑟听得出来，因为在他们中间用通事传话。
verses.en: (Now[NOTE:1] they did not know that Joseph could understand them,[NOTE:2] for he was speaking through an interpreter.)[NOTE:3]
notes: The disjunctive clause provides supplemental information that is important to the story.
“was listening.” The brothers were not aware that Joseph could understand them as they spoke the preceding words in their native language.

Heb “for [there was] an interpreter between them.” On the meaning of the word here translated “interpreter” see HALOT 590 s.v. מֵלִיץ and M. A. Canney, “The Hebrew melis (Prov IX 12; Gen XLII 2-3),” AJSL 40 (1923/24): 135-37.
verses.commentary:
42:23 "They did not know, however, that Joseph understood for there was an interpreter between them"
They were speaking Hebrew; Joseph apparently only spoke Egyptian to them through an interpreter. Again, this
was part of the disguise until he was able to ascertain whether his brothers had overcome the biases which
caused them to sin against him over twenty years earlier.

This Hebrew VERB translated "there was an interpreter" (BDB 539, KB 529,
Hiphil PARTICIPLE) usually denotes scorn or mockery. In the Hiphil stem it
denotes

- derision, Job 16:20; Ps. 119:51

- interpreter, here an envoy, 2 Chr. 32:31

All of the uses of this VERB in the OT occur in a negative context (cf. NIDOTTE,
vol. 2, p. 799).

verses.zh: 约瑟转身退去，哭了一场，又回来对他们说话，就从他们中间挑出西缅来，在他们眼前把他捆绑。
verses.en: He turned away from them and wept. When he turned around and spoke to them again,[NOTE:1] he had Simeon taken[NOTE:2] from them and tied up[NOTE:3] before their eyes.
notes: Heb “and he turned to them and spoke to them.”
Heb “took Simeon.” This was probably done at Joseph’s command, however; the grand vizier of Egypt would not have personally seized a prisoner.
Heb “and he bound him.” See the note on the preceding verb “taken.”
verses.commentary:
42:24 "wept" Joseph was apparently a sensitive man (cf. Gen. 43:30; 45:14,15).

▣ "he took Simeon from them and bound him before their eyes" Obviously Reuben, the firstborn,
was the leader of the group and had apparently tried to help Joseph, so the obvious choice was Simeon. He
was the second born and many commentators believe that fierce anger seen in his destruction of the men of
Shechem (cf. Genesis 34) may have involved him in the original plot to hurt Joseph.

verses.zh: 约瑟吩咐人把粮食装满他们的器具，把各人的银子归还在各人的口袋里，又给他们路上用的食物，人就照他的话办了。
verses.en: Then Joseph gave orders to fill[NOTE:1] their bags with grain, to return each man’s money to his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. His orders were carried out.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and they filled.” The clause appears to be elliptical; one expects “Joseph gave orders to fill…and they filled.” See GKC 386 §120.f.

Heb “and he did for them so.” Joseph would appear to be the subject of the singular verb. If the text is retained, the statement seems to be a summary of the preceding, more detailed statement. However, some read the verb as plural, “and they did for them so.” In this case the statement indicates that Joseph’s subordinates carried out his orders. Another alternative is to read the singular verb as passive (with unspecified subject), “and this was done for them so” (cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
42:25-29 The nine brothers were afraid that this would jeopardize Simeon's release. The level of
their concern is expressed in

- their hearts sank, Gen. 42:28 (lit. "their hearts went out from them"), BDB 422, KB 425,
Qal IMPERFECT with waw

- they turned trembling to one another, Gen. 42:28, BDB 353, KB 350, Qal
IMPERFECT with waw, cf. Gen. 27:33; 1 Sam. 16:4; 21:1; 1 Kgs. 1:49

verses.zh: 他们就把粮食驮在驴上，离开那里去了。
verses.en: So they loaded their grain on their donkeys and left.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and they went from there.”

verses.zh: 到了住宿的地方，他们中间有一个人打开口袋，要拿料喂驴，才看见自己的银子仍在口袋里，
verses.en: When one of them[NOTE:1] opened his sack to get feed for his donkey at their resting place,[NOTE:2] he saw his money in the mouth of his sack.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and the one.” The article indicates that the individual is vivid in the mind of the narrator, yet it is not important to identify him by name.
Heb “at the lodging place.”

Heb “and look, it [was] in the mouth of his sack.” By the use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”), the narrator invites the reader to look through the eyes of the character and thereby draws attention to the money.
verses.commentary:
42:27 "sack" There are two different Hebrew terms translated "sack" in this verse.

- "sack" (BDB 974), which is a common term for "sackcloth" (used here)

- "sack" (BDB 607), which is found only in this account about Joseph and his brothers. It refers
to a sack carrying grain.

The answer for the use of the two terms may be that one refers to a money pouch (cf. NIDOTTE,
vol. 3, p. 843) and the other a sack for grain (cf. James W. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible,
p. 49).

verses.zh: 就对弟兄们说：「我的银子归还了，看哪，仍在我口袋里！」他们就提心吊胆，战战兢兢地彼此说：「这是　神向我们做甚么呢？」
verses.en: He said to his brothers, “My money was returned! Here it is in my sack!” They were dismayed;[NOTE:1] they turned trembling to one another[NOTE:2] and said, “What in the world has God done to us?”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and their heart went out.” Since this expression is used only here, the exact meaning is unclear. The following statement suggests that it may refer to a sudden loss of emotional strength, so “They were dismayed” adequately conveys the meaning (cf. NRSV); NIV has “Their hearts sank.”
Heb “and they trembled, a man to his neighbor.”
Heb “What is this God has done to us?” The demonstrative pronoun (“this”) adds emphasis to the question.
verses.commentary:
42:28 "What is this that God has done to us" They still were feeling the divine judgment for their
actions against Joseph.

verses.zh: 他们来到迦南地、他们的父亲雅各那里，将所遭遇的事都告诉他，说：
verses.en: They returned to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan and told him all the things that had happened to them, saying,
verses.commentary: 42:29-34 The nine brothers relate to their father, Jacob, all that happened in Egypt.

verses.zh: 「那地的主对我们说严厉的话，把我们当作窥探那地的奸细。
verses.en: “The man, the lord of the land, spoke harshly to us and treated us[NOTE:1] as if we were[NOTE:2] spying on the land.
notes: Heb “made us.”
The words “if we were” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 我们对他说：『我们是诚实人，并不是奸细。
verses.en: But we said to him, ‘We are honest men; we are not spies!

verses.zh: 我们本是弟兄十二人，都是一个父亲的儿子，有一个没有了，顶小的如今同我们的父亲在迦南地。』
verses.en: We are from a family of twelve brothers; we are the sons of one father.[NOTE:1] One is no longer alive,[NOTE:2] and the youngest is with our father at this time[NOTE:3] in the land of Canaan.’
notes: Heb “twelve [were] we, brothers, sons of our father [are] we.”
Heb “the one is not.”
Heb “today.”

verses.zh: 那地的主对我们说：『若要我知道你们是诚实人，可以留下你们中间的一个人在我这里，你们可以带着粮食回去，救你们家里的饥荒。
verses.en: “Then the man, the lord of the land, said to us, ‘This is how I will find out if you are honest men. Leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain[NOTE:1] for your hungry households and go.
notes: The word “grain” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 把你们的小兄弟带到我这里来，我便知道你们不是奸细，乃是诚实人。这样，我就把你们的弟兄交给你们，你们也可以在这地做买卖。』」
verses.en: But bring your youngest brother back to me so I will know[NOTE:1] that you are honest men and not spies.[NOTE:2] Then I will give your brother back to you and you may move about freely in the land.’”[NOTE:3]
notes: After the imperative, the cohortative with prefixed vav indicates purpose/result.
Heb “that you are not spies, that you are honest men.”

Joseph’s brothers soften the news considerably, making it sound like Simeon was a guest of Joseph (Leave one of your brothers with me) instead of being bound in prison. They do not mention the threat of death and do not at this time speak of the money in the one sack.
verses.commentary:
42:34 "you may trade in the land" This VERB (BDB 695, KB 749, Qal
IMPERFECT) is translated "trade" (cf. Gen. 23:16), but its use in Gen. 34:10 implies a
meaning of "travel about freely." It is possible that it refers specifically to returning to Egypt for
more grain when necessary (cf. Gen. 43:2).

verses.zh: 后来他们倒口袋，不料，各人的银包都在口袋里；他们和父亲看见银包就都害怕。
verses.en: When they were emptying their sacks, there was each man’s bag of money in his sack! When they and their father saw the bags of money, they were afraid.
verses.commentary:
42:35-38 The family discusses the situation and what to do. They decide to do nothing for the moment.

42:35 The difference between Gen. 42:27 and Gen. 42:35 is "one" of them in Gen. 42:27 and "they"
in Gen. 42:35. This is not a doublet, but an intensification of the problem that had frightened them
earlier (cf. Gen. 42:28).

▣ "dismayed" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

verses.zh: 他们的父亲雅各对他们说：「你们使我丧失我的儿子：「约瑟没有了，西缅也没有了，你们又要将便雅悯带去；这些事都归到我身上了。」
verses.en: Their father Jacob said to them, “You are making me childless! Joseph is gone.[NOTE:1] Simeon is gone.[NOTE:2] And now you want to take[NOTE:3] Benjamin! Everything is against me.”
notes: Heb “is not.”
Heb “is not.”
The nuance of the imperfect verbal form is desiderative here.
verses.commentary:
42:36 "You have bereaved me of my children; Joseph is no more, and Simeon is no more, and you would
take Benjamin; all these things are against me" Notice that Jacob takes the occurrences as a personal
affront. There seems to be an implied accusation that the brothers were somehow involved in the loss of
Joseph.

verses.zh: 流便对他父亲说：「我若不带他回来交给你，你可以杀我的两个儿子。只管把他交在我手里，我必带他回来交给你。」
verses.en: Then Reuben said to his father, “You may[NOTE:1] put my two sons to death if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my care[NOTE:2] and I will bring him back to you.”
notes: The nuance of the imperfect verbal form is permissive here.
Heb “my hand.”
verses.commentary:
42:37 "Then Reuben spoke to his father, saying" This is really a dumb offer! Why would Jacob, because
of the loss of his sons, kill his grandsons?! It was an attempt by Reuben to assure his father, but it did
quite the opposite. Jacob would wait until

- Judah's offer in Gen. 43:8-9

- the reality of no food to finally allow Benjamin to go with them

verses.zh: 雅各说：「我的儿子不可与你们一同下去；他哥哥死了，只剩下他，他若在你们所行的路上遭害，那便是你们使我白发苍苍、悲悲惨惨地下阴间去了。」
verses.en: But Jacob[NOTE:1] replied, “My son will not go down there with you, for his brother is dead and he alone is left.[NOTE:2] If an accident happens to him on the journey you have to make, then you will bring down my gray hair[NOTE:3] in sorrow to the grave.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The expression he alone is left meant that (so far as Jacob knew) Benjamin was the only surviving child of his mother Rachel.
The expression bring down my gray hair is figurative, using a part for the whole—they would put Jacob in the grave. But the gray head signifies a long life of worry and trouble.
Heb “to Sheol,” the dwelling place of the dead.
verses.commentary:
42:38 "Sheol" This is the OT term used for the place of the dead. The doctrine of the afterlife
is somewhat veiled in the OT, but it is obvious that they believed in an afterlife where families were
together.

It is true that it was a shadowy, joyless state, but a conscious state nonetheless. The
term Sheol is translated by the term Hades in the NT. Apparently all human beings went to
this holding place of the dead. For that reason the rabbis speculate that there is a righteous part and
a wicked part of Hades.
